title: The world born of hunger
hook: a second creation story: at first there was nothing, covered by death, which is hunger, and hunger made the world
carry: the world is food and eater; offer first
tomorrow: the gods and demons and the breath

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashvamedha: the Brihadaranyaka opened by seeing the sacrificial horse as the cosmos. Your line was the whole world is the sacred offering.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA — THE WHOLE WORLD IS THE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: In the beginning there was nothing here at all. All this was covered by death. And death, it says, is hunger. That's the first sentence of the Brihadaranyaka's second section. Twenty days ago, Uddalaka told his son a calmer story: in the beginning there was Being alone, and it thought, let me be many. Two great Upanishads, two creation stories. Hindu tradition has kept them both, side by side.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, NOTHING.` → `TWENTY DAYS AGO: BEING ALONE, CALM.` → `TWO STORIES, KEPT SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit: naiveha kimcanagra asit, mrityunaivedam avritam asit, ashanayaya. Ashanaya hi mrityuh: for hunger is death. Then death does something. It makes a mind, thinking: let me have a self. It moves about, chanting praise, and from its praise water arises. The froth on the water hardens into the earth. Death toils, and from its heat, fire is born. Through the mind it joins with speech, and the year is born. Death opens its mouth to swallow the newborn year, and the year cries out, bhan! That cry becomes speech. Death thinks: if I eat this, I'll have less food. So instead, through speech, it brings forth everything: the verses of the Vedas, the rituals, people, animals. And whatever it brings forth, it begins to eat. Then death's body swells, and the text plays on a word: the swollen one, ashva, the horse. Yesterday's horse, back again. A few pages later the same Upanishad sums it up: this whole world is just food and the eater of food. That's the teaching to keep. Many teachers read it this way: eating is never only eating; it's part of the great sacrifice the world is made of. Many teachers connect this to what Hindu families do every day: before eating, they offer the food first, at the home shrine or with a short prayer, and what comes back is prasad, a gift. Hunger runs all the way down. Offering first is how a Hindu turns that hunger into worship.
screen: `FOR HUNGER IS DEATH.` · `THE NEWBORN YEAR CRIES OUT: BHAN!` · `ALL THIS IS FOOD AND EATER.` · `OFFERED FIRST, RETURNED AS PRASAD.` · then, large: `OFFER FIRST.`

segments.voice: Notice any hunger in you right now: for food, for your phone, for something to happen. Don't act on it; watch it rise. Then picture your next meal in front of you. If you pray, offer it silently first, the way many Hindu families do, to God, to Krishna, to whoever you call on, and only then imagine taking the first bite. If you don't pray, simply pause before it and give thanks for everyone and everything that became this food.
Ashanaya, hunger. The Brihadaranyaka's creation: nothing, covered by death, which is hunger, and from that hunger, mind, water, earth, fire, speech and a world of food and eaters.
Your line: the world is food and eater; offer first. Tomorrow, the gods go looking for a singer. That's day three hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 361 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GODS AND DEMONS AND THE BREATH.`

original.note: Sanskrit aśanāyā: hunger, the wish to eat. aśanāyā hi mṛtyuḥ: for hunger is death.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy creation myth.
what it means: hunger is the root of the world, and everything eats and is eaten. many teachers connect this to why Hindus offer food before eating.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 1.2, full of wordplay (arka from arc and ka; ashva from ashvat, swelled), and it explains the horse sacrifice of 1.1.

notes: Sanskrit of 1.2.1 in simplified transliteration (naiveha kiṃcanāgra āsīn mṛtyunaivedam āvṛtam āsīd aśanāyayā, aśanāyā hi mṛtyuḥ); only the first phrase is listed as quoted, the rest appears in the voice from the same verse. Confirm.

Story details paraphrased: water from death's worship (arka wordplay), froth becoming earth, fire from its toil, union of mind and speech producing the year, the cry 'bhan' becoming speech (1.2.4), aditi from 'ad' (omitted), ashva from 'ashvat' (1.2.7). Confirm each.
